processing: Fully oxidised gongfu black tea: withered, rolled, oxidised and dried, with drying heat around 90 to 100°C.
harvest_season: Spring lots are generally the most prized; cheaper grades also use summer and autumn leaf.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine, dark glossy strands with chrysanthemum-yellow down in tippy grades.
appearance_wet: Typically plump coppery-red leaf and bud.
taste_profile: Rich aroma and a full, mellow body; one traditional-style lot shows malt, fruit, tang and stony minerality rather than plain sweetness.

brewing.notes: Keep the first steeps short, since large-leaf tea gets strong fast. Western-style, use about 2.5 g per 250 ml for 2 to 3 minutes.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year and grade, from gold-bud spring lots to everyday summer and autumn leaf, and generally drunk within a year or two. Some lots state the exact picking date. Dian Hong is not a vintage tea in the way pu-erh is.
description:
Fengqing is where Dian Hong began, so tea from here is the reference point for Yunnan black tea. The county, in Lincang prefecture, was called Shunning when the first trial batch was made, and its name is also a registered certification trademark for the tea.

The method is the classic four steps of withering, rolling, oxidation and drying, applied to large-leaf plants. Dian Hong is valued for strength, body and freshness, and golden tip is the mark of the better grades. In Fengqing that down leans towards chrysanthemum yellow rather than the deeper gold of southern Yunnan.

A good lot pours a bright deep red, smelling rich and full. Tippy grades are soft and sweet, while leafier ones have more malt and grip. Short steeps keep the sweetness in front.

Buying means reading the grade: the name covers everything from gold needles to low-priced summer and autumn leaf. Ask for the harvest date, and do not assume that wild or ancient tree claims on a low-priced tea are accurate.
history:
In 1938 the tea expert Feng Shaoqiu surveyed Yunnan and made black tea samples in what is now Fengqing, then Shunning. Hong Kong buyers praised them. In 1939 gongfu black tea was made at the Shunning Experimental Tea Factory under the name Yunhong, and on 9 April 1940 the name became Dian Hong.

The Shunning factory was the forerunner of Fengqing's tea factory. Dian Hong production techniques are listed as intangible cultural heritage, with Fengqing as a main home of the craft.
